source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Example of How to Trade a Breakout

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: BullTrendBar
candidates.quote: Both bars 14 and 15 were strong bull trend bars with good-sized bodies and without significant tails.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the current bar is a bull trend bar (closed up, body is most of its range).
notes: Same construction as RP1-02/R08-01; the dedup pass should merge all trend-bar primitives across chapters.

candidates.name: TrailingStopBelowRecentStrongTrendBar
candidates.quote: Many traders who bought the bar 15 close might have raised their stops to below bar 17 once it closed because they would not have wanted the market to fall below such a strong bull trend bar.
candidates.description: While long, trail the protective stop to just below the low of the most recent large-range bull trend bar, instead of a fixed distance.
candidates.pseudocode: strongBarLow = low[k] for the most recent bar k where BullTrendBar[k] && (high[k] - low[k]) >= rangeMultiple * atr(atrLookback); low[0] <= strongBarLow - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: must remember the most recent qualifying trend bar's low as cross-bar state

candidates.name: TrailingStopInMicroMeasuringGap
candidates.quote: many might have put their protective stops in the micro measuring gap created by the bar 17 breakout. The low of bar 18 was above the high of bar 16, and this gap is a sign of strength.
candidates.description: Trail the protective stop into the most recent micro measuring gap: a two-bar-apart gap where a bar's low sits above the high of the bar two bars earlier.
candidates.pseudocode: gapLow = low[g] for the most recent g where low[g] > high[g + 2]; low[0] <= gapLow - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: variable-offset gap detection plus persisted state for the most recent gap found

candidates.name: AddOnDuringContinuingSpike
candidates.quote: Many experienced traders use spikes to press their trades. They add to their longs as the spike continues up, because they know that the spike has an exceptional trader's equation.
candidates.description: While already long and the spike continues (each new bar is another significant trend bar making a higher high), add to the position rather than waiting for a pullback.
candidates.book_order_type: market order, add to existing position

complexity.reason: position-state-dependent add-on entry; the engine may need to model this as a distinct scale-in placement

notes: Flag for the authoring pass: this is a pyramiding/scale-in rule, not a fresh-position entry; check whether the pane system supports adding to an open position.

candidates.name: RestingStopAboveSpikeHigh
candidates.quote: traders needed to place their worst-case entry buy stop orders above the spike high ... They needed to place a buy stop at one tick above the bar 19 high, in case the trend quickly resumed.
candidates.description: While flat or looking to enter with-trend during a strong spike, keep a resting buy stop one tick above the recent spike high active, so a sudden resumption is not missed even if no pullback entry ever triggers.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the spike high

candidates.name: BreakoutEntryRequiresPriorTrendStrength
candidates.quote: There was good buying pressure all of the way up from the bar 5 low, as seen by many strong bull trend bars, little overlap, and only a few bear trend bars ... the reward is greater, the risk is smaller, and the probability of success is higher when entering on pullbacks.
candidates.description: Filter: only take the raw stop entry above a swing high (skipping the pullback entry) once recent bars already show strong with-trend character; otherwise prefer waiting for a pullback entry.

complexity.reason: fixed-length window counters over a bar-classification primitive

candidates.name: FailedBearBreakoutBullBodyConfirmation
candidates.quote: if there is instead a bull body, even a small one, the odds of a failed breakout attempt become higher ... The bar before bar 12 was a large bear trend bar ... Bulls bought the close of the bear trend bar ... Once they saw that bar 12 had a bull close, they bought the close of bar 12 and above its high.
candidates.description: After a bear trend bar in a bull trend, if the very next bar has any bull body (even a small one), treat the bear breakout as likely failed and buy its close and above its high.
candidates.pseudocode: close[1] < open[1] && (open[1] - close[1]) >= bodyFraction * (high[1] - low[1]) && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the close of the confirming bar and above its high
notes: First target = the bear bar's high; second target = a measured move equal to its height, same construction as RP1-09/RP1-10.

candidates.name: NearEmaAugmentsReversalOdds
candidates.quote: especially when the bar is at the moving average in a bull trend.
candidates.description: Filter: the failed-bear-breakout confirmation (R01-07) is more reliable when the confirming bar sits at or near the EMA.

complexity.reason: needs an EMA and an ATR-scaled distance band

candidates.name: FirstPullbackAfterNewLegUnlikelyToReverse
candidates.quote: Why would experienced traders ever buy back their highly profitable shorts when the first pullback in a strong trend usually fails? ... Profit taking is the cause of the first pullback in any strong trend.
candidates.description: Filter: the first pullback after a fresh, strong trend leg begins rarely reverses the trend; increase confidence buying it (with-trend) rather than fading it.

complexity.reason: needs a persistent counter of pullbacks since the current leg began

candidates.name: SignalBarBodyMatchesTradeDirection
candidates.quote: The signal bar is more reliable when it has a bull body.
candidates.description: Filter: a breakout-pullback signal bar is more reliable when its own body closes in the trade direction (a bull body for a long setup) rather than a bear or doji body.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (signal-quality filter, applied to the signal bar of some other setup)
notes: Generic gate meant to sit alongside H1/H2/ii/outside-bar setups (bar 8 high 2, bar 14 outside up, bar 20 ii, bar 23/25 high 2 mentioned in this chapter); those pattern definitions belong to later chapters.

candidates.name: MovingAverageGapBar
candidates.quote: Bar 12 was a second-entry moving average gap bar short setup ... It had a bear body and was also a 20-gap bar short setup
candidates.description: Shared primitive: a bar whose entire range sits on one side of the EMA without touching it — used as evidence of countertrend strength and as a stand-alone signal bar for second-entry setups.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop below the gap bar's low (short case)

complexity.reason: needs an EMA plus a whole-bar comparison against it

notes: ‘Second entry’ and ‘20-gap bar’ are named but not defined in this chapter; the ranges book's own chapters on first-moving-average gap bars and 20-gap bars (outside the mining scope here) should supply the full definitions.

candidates.name: GapMidpointOrFirstLegHighMeasuredMove
candidates.quote: The low of the bar after the breakout bar and the high of the bar 11 breakout point created a breakout gap. Either its middle or the high of the first leg up to bar 11 could lead to a measured move up.
candidates.description: After a breakout gap forms, project a measured move from whichever of two anchors is nearer — the gap's midpoint or the high of the first leg up to the breakout — and exit when price reaches it.
candidates.pseudocode: gapMid = (low[b + 1] + high[b]) / 2; anchor = min(gapMid, legHigh); target = anchor + (anchor - legStart); high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs the breakout bar, the first-leg high, and the leg start all remembered as state

notes: Same family as RP1-07 and chapter 8's measured-move targets (R08-05/09/10); the dedup pass should merge.

candidates.name: ThirdConsecutiveClimaxLateSessionAvoidCountertrend
candidates.quote: Bar 24 was a two-bar bull spike and the third consecutive buy climax without a correction. There was not enough time left in the day for a 10-bar, two-legged correction, so not many bears were willing to short it.
candidates.description: Filter: after the Nth consecutive buy climax, avoid initiating a countertrend short if too little of the session remains for a full multi-bar, two-legged correction to complete.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter blocking a countertrend entry)

complexity.reason: climax counting has no agreed mechanical definition, compounded with a session-time gate

notes: Same climax-counting concept as RP1-14/RP1-15, restated with an explicit end-of-session constraint.

rejected.quote: A trader needs to be aggressive when the market is offering trades with strong trader's equations. He also needs to trade little or not at all when it does not, like in a tight trading range.
rejected.reason: pure discretion with no bar-level test given

rejected.quote: Bear spikes, especially on daily charts, can be due to news items, but most fail to have follow-through, and the longer-term bullish fundamentals win out
rejected.reason: requires knowing news causation, which the engine cannot have; the mechanizable fade-the-spike behavior is already covered by RP1-08/R01-07

rejected.quote: It had a bear body and was also a 20-gap bar short setup (discussed later in this book).
rejected.reason: named pattern with no bar-level test defined in this chapter; pure forward reference

rejected.quote: you can go to the Wiley website (www.wiley.com/go/tradingranges) and either view the chart or print it out
rejected.reason: meta text about the book itself, not a trading statement

chapter_summary: A worked chart example rather than a rules list, but it yields concrete mechanics beyond the Part I intro: two variant trailing-stop schemes tied to recent strong bars and micro measuring gaps, a resting last-ditch stop above the spike high (which reduces to the catalog's HighestHighBreakout), a pyramiding add-on rule, a two-bar failed-bear-breakout confirmation with an EMA-proximity booster, and several context filters (prior-trend-strength gate on raw breakout entries, first-pullback-is-safe, signal-bar body direction, climax-plus-session-time gate). It also names, without defining, 'second entry', 'moving average gap bar', and '20-gap bar' setups that belong to later chapters of this book; MovingAverageGapBar (R01-11) is mined here as a best-effort primitive since enough is said to mechanize it.
